boon-of-terror|frhof.summary: Without a built-in way to make enemies Frightened, there’s very little value here. There are a few subclass features that can do the job, but that’s not much.

boon-of-the-bright-sun|frhof.name: Boon of the Bright Sun
boon-of-the-bright-sun|frhof.summary: Give yourself and your allies 10 Temporary Hit Points each turn. Boon of Bountiful Health is a good complement to this, giving you extra THP whenever you gain any.

boon-of-the-furious-storm|frhof.name: Boon of the Furious Storm
boon-of-the-furious-storm|frhof.summary: Resistance/immunity to two damage types is nice. The Disadvantage mechanic won’t matter often, but it applies to Lightning Arrow. Of course, Lightning Arrow is terrible, so that doesn’t really matter.

boon-of-the-night-spirit|phb.name: Boon of the Night Spirit
boon-of-the-night-spirit|phb.summary: Excellent on a stealthy character like the Ranger. However, remember that a lot of things are an Action, so it’s very easy to break this invisibility. Notable examples that people easily overlook include Hide, Search, and Study.

boon-of-the-soul-drinker|frhof.name: Boon of the Soul Drinker
boon-of-the-soul-drinker|frhof.summary: Resistance to two damage types. The healing is negligible. Take Boon of Fortitude instead.

boon-of-truesight|phb.name: Boon of Truesight
boon-of-truesight|phb.summary: Probably your only option for handling invisible enemies, but the ability scores are hard unless you’re building around Druidic Warrior. If you’ve made it this far, your party is covering for you or you’ve found a creative solution.

club|unknown.name: Club
club|unknown.summary: Light. Just use light hammers. If you’re trying to build around Shillelagh and two weapons, you’re going to struggle because you simply won’t have enough Bonus Actions to make it work.

dagger|unknown.name: Dagger
dagger|unknown.summary: Finesse, Light, Thrown, and Nick mastery. Pair with a shortsword and take Piercer.

light-hammer|unknown.name: Light Hammer
light-hammer|unknown.summary: Light, Thrown, and Nick mastery. There isn’t a better bludgeoning option for two-weapon fighting, so, if you want to use Crusher, you’ll probably use two of these. Unfortunately, this doesn’t have Finesse, so it’s only viable for Strength-based builds.

handaxe|unknown.name: Handaxe
handaxe|unknown.summary: A go-to choice for your primary weapon when using two-weapon fighting. It also has the Thrown property, allowing you to more easily pivot to ranged combat. Unfortunately, this doesn’t have Finesse, so it’s only viable for Strength-based builds.

scimitar|unknown.name: Scimitar
scimitar|unknown.summary: The go-to secondary weapon for two-weapon fighting since it has the largest damage die of any weapon with the Nick property, but if you’re taking Piercer you’ll want to use a dagger instead.

shortsword|unknown.name: Shortsword
shortsword|unknown.summary: Finesse, Light, Vex mastery, and works with the Piercer feat. Pair with a dagger.

hand-crossbow|function.name: Hand Crossbow
hand-crossbow|function.summary: Two-weapon fighting via Crossbow Expert, but without the Nick property the additional attack eats your Bonus Action, so you won’t be able to use it every turn. You may have better results throwing daggers or hand axes.ezstandalone.cmd.push(function () { ezstandalone.showAds(195); });

longbow|unknown.name: Longbow
longbow|unknown.summary: The go-to weapon for ranged builds.

musket|unknown.name: Musket
musket|unknown.summary: This has the Loading property, which will present a problem as soon as you get Extra Attack. With the Gunner feat, this is a linear upgrade from the Longbow, at least in terms of damage. Range might be an issue occasionally, but if that worries you, take Sharpshooter.

pistol|unknown.name: Pistol
pistol|unknown.summary: Good damage for a one-handed weapon, and the Vex mastery. Advantage from Vex will make your DPR with a pistol better than DPR with a musket so long as you’re repeatedly attacking the same target. If you have enough gold, you can bring a whole bunch of loaded pistols and repeatedly draw and fire them instead of reloading. Or you could take the Gunner feat.

studded-leather|unknown.name: Studded Leather
studded-leather|unknown.summary: Dexterity-based builds should grab studded leather as soon as they hit 18 Dexterity.

half-plate|unknown.name: Half Plate
half-plate|unknown.summary: Druidic Warrior builds don’t need as much Dexterity as typical rangers, so medium armor is a good choice.

shield|unknown.name: Shield
shield|unknown.summary: +2 AC is huge in this game. Typical Rangers nearly always go for two-weapon fighting or ranged weapons, but Druidic Warrior builds can easily accommodate a shield.

cleric|unknown.name: Cleric
cleric|unknown.summary: A single level of Cleric can get you heavy armor proficiency and a bunch of Wisdom-based spellcasting. Plus, you can do this at any level rather than being forced to do it at 1st level to get heavy armor like you must with martial classes. This is a great replacement for Druidic Warrior.

druid|unknown.name: Druid
druid|unknown.summary: You need to take at least 3 levels before you get anything worthwhile that you can’t match with either a level of Cleric or Druidic Warrior.

fighter|unknown.name: Fighter
fighter|unknown.summary: Starting with 1 level in Fighter to get proficiency in Constitution saves and heavy armor proficient is fantastic. You also get more Weapon Master and another Fighting Style.

monk|unknown.name: Monk
monk|unknown.summary: If you have 14 Wisdom, the Monk’s Unarmored Defense will match Studded Leather, making it a fantastic defense for most Ranger builds. Martial Arts offers a good way to get additional attacks, though it will compete for your Bonus Action with applying Hunter’s Mark and casting other combat spells, which might be frustrating. Martial Arts also lets you use Dexterity for many non-Finesse melee weapons, dramatically expanding your weapon options.

rogue|unknown.name: Rogue
rogue|unknown.summary: 1 level for Expertise and more Weapon Mastery. 2 levels for Cunning Action. Sneak Attack won’t be a significant improvement to your damage otuput, but don’t let that deter you.

create-bonfire|eepc-xgte.name: Create Bonfire
create-bonfire|eepc-xgte.summary: Good damage and cheap area control, but it requires Concentration, and it’s not good enough to justify over concentrating on Hunter’s Mark.

elementalism|unknown.name: Elementalism
elementalism|unknown.summary: Very flavorful, but almost totally useless.

frostbite|eepc-xgte.name: Frostbite
frostbite|eepc-xgte.summary: Low damage for a cantrip (d6-based), but the big appeal is Disadvantage on the target’s next weapon attack. Unfortunately, it works on Constitution saving throws, and those tend to be relatively high compared to other saving throws.

guidance|phb.name: Guidance
guidance|phb.summary: Really good, but you likely can’t make room for it.

gust|eepc-xgte.name: Gust
gust|eepc-xgte.summary: This spell is almost totally useless.

infestation|xgte.name: Infestation
infestation|xgte.summary: The forced movement is the main appeal, and you can get that from Weapon Mastery much more reliably.

magic-stone|eepc-xgte.name: Magic Stone
magic-stone|eepc-xgte.summary: 1d6+Wis damage. You get Extra Attack, and this doesn’t consume Concentration, so it can work with Hunter’s Mark. You can also fire the stones from a sling to use Weapon Mastery. The biggest issue is spending a Bonus Action every 3 shots, which will compete heavily with Hunter’s Mark. It’s doable, but there will be turns where you won’t have Hunter’s Mark in place because you needed to refresh Magic Stone.

message|phb.name: Message
message|phb.summary: Situational. Use this to send messages without revealing your position.

mold-earth|eepc-xgte.name: Mold Earth
mold-earth|eepc-xgte.summary: You know what else can do this? A shovel. Sure, shoveling will take a long time, but you get at most 3 Cantrips (5 with Circle of the Land), and if you can replace a Cantrip with a mundane item it’s probably a bad Cantrip. The only important function is to create difficult terrain, but you’re limited to two ongoing effects, which means you only get two 5-foot squares. And, again, you could do that with a shovel. You’re about as likely to use this in combat as you are to use a shovel, too.

poison-spray|phb.name: Poison Spray
poison-spray|phb.summary: This highest damage die for Cantrips, at least until Toll the Dead came along. Poison spray has serious problems: 10 ft. range, and it works on a Constitution saving throw, so enemies will frequently resist it.

primal-savagery|xgte.name: Primal Savagery
primal-savagery|xgte.summary: Shillelagh will be more effective, so get Shillelagh unless you desperately need an empty hand for some reason.

produce-flame|phb.name: Produce Flame
produce-flame|phb.summary: A decent attack Cantrip, it notably also allows you to hold the flame and carry it around as a light source. The action economy is annoying, though: you need to spend a Bonus Action to activate the spell, then an Action to actually attack. You could walk around with this running to keep it ready, but there’s not much reason to do when Starry Wisp exists.

resistance|phb.name: Resistance
resistance|phb.summary: Considerably more difficult to use than Guidance. Your best bet is to throw this on an ally before going into combat, but if you have that luxury you should be casting a better Concentration spell.

shape-water|eepc-xgte.name: Shape Water
shape-water|eepc-xgte.summary: See our Practical Guide to Shape Water for more on how great Shape Water is.

shillelagh|phb.name: Shillelagh
shillelagh|phb.summary: Basically the reason Druidic Warrior exists. In a lot of ways, this cantrip perfectly exemplifies the trade you’re making with Druidic Warrior. You get to turn a club or quarterstaff into a longsword equivalent using your Wisdom modifier. Consider grabbing Polearm Master, too.

spare-the-dying|unknown.name: Spare the Dying
spare-the-dying|unknown.summary: The only benefit to Spare the Dying is that it has 15-foot range, and that’s so little range that it’s hardly worth considering. Buy a Healer’s Kit and walk the 15 feet if you need to stabilize an ally as an Action.

starry-wisp|unknown.name: Starry Wisp
starry-wisp|unknown.summary: Decent damage, good damage type, and it prevents enemies from hiding or turning invisibile. But it won’t keep up with other options since you get Extra Attack.

thorn-whip|phb.name: Thorn Whip
thorn-whip|phb.summary: The damage is fine, but the real appeal is the pull effect. 10 feet may not seem like much, but its enough to pull enemies off of ledges, to pull low-flying enemies into melee, to pull enemies into an area control effect like Create Bonfire or Wall of Fire, to pull enemies out of a grapple, or in a pinch you can pull an ally out of a dangerous location (albeit at the price of some friendly fire).

thunderclap|eepc-xgte.name: Thunderclap
thunderclap|eepc-xgte.summary: Damaging every creature within 5 feet of you is great if you’re in melee facing numerous enemies. Even with Extra Attack you will deal more damage with this against three or more foes than you could with a weapon. See our article on Melee Cantrips vs. Extra Attack for a breakdown of the math comparing melee Cantrips to normal martial attacks.

absorb-elements|xgte.name: Absorb Elements
absorb-elements|xgte.summary: You get spellcasting later and slower than anyone else, so you have very few options for protecting yourself from non-weapon damage. This will handle that issue, but it will eat your spell slots quickly so be sure to eliminate the source of the elemental damage as quickly as possible so that you don’t run through your spell slots too quickly. The biggest challenge for Absorb Elements is that is has Somatic components, which require a free hand. By default, this means that two-weapon fighting builds and sword-and-board builds will be unable to use this unless you’re dilligent about drawing and stowing your weapon, which both makes opportunity attacks hard and only allows Absorb Elements every other round. Unfortunately, the only way around this is War Caster.

alarm|phb.name: Alarm
alarm|phb.summary: Great to cast as a Ritual when you’re resting, but .

animal-friendship|phb.name: Animal Friendship
animal-friendship|phb.summary: Arguably easier than proficiency in Animal Handling, but it will become obsolete once beasts disappear around CR 10.

beast-bond|eepc.name: Beast Bond
beast-bond|eepc.summary: Largely useless. Even for Beast Master Rangers, your beast has 8 Intelligence, so it doesn’t qualify.

buzzing-bee|drops.name: Buzzing Bee
buzzing-bee|drops.summary: Long range, no save, and it inhibits stealth, Perception, and Concentration. It’s somehow both broadly useful but also very difficult to justify. Buzzing Bee prevents the target from benefiting from invisibility, which means that they can’t benefit from hiding. But you need to be able to see them, which means that most enemies that rely on invisiblity won’t care. This doesn’t allow a save like Faerie Fire does, but Faerie Fire also don’t require you to see the target, and Faerie Fire also works as a great support option even when enemies aren’t invisibile. Imposing Disadvantage on Perception may be helpful for sneaking past enemies, but since Buzzing Bee is single-target and has a Verbal component, which makes it difficult to use in most stealth situations. The Concentration option may be helpful against enemy spellcasters, but for the same action cost and spell slot you can use any number of other spells that could actually break Concentration.ezstandalone.cmd.push(function () { ezstandalone.showAds(179); });

cure-wounds|phb.name: Cure Wounds
cure-wounds|phb.summary: Rangers don’t have as many spell slots as a full caster, so using your precious few slots on healing can be difficult. However, someone in the party needs to be able to heal the primary healer if they fall unconscious, and you’re someone.

detect-magic|phb.name: Detect Magic
detect-magic|phb.summary: Ideally someone in the party who can cast more spells than you will handle this, but sometimes you don’t really have a choice. Fortunately, you can cast it as a Ritual to avoid spending precious spell slots.

detect-poison-and-disease|phb.name: Detect Poison and Disease
detect-poison-and-disease|phb.summary: Very situational, and unless you can also cast Protection From Poison, there’s little you can do about it anyway other than physically avoiding the threat. Fortunately, this can be cast as a Ritual.

ensnaring-strike|phb.name: Ensnaring Strike
ensnaring-strike|phb.summary: Almost exclusive to Rangers, Ensnaring Strike is a great way to handle single targets that are causing you problems, especially if the target is a melee monster. Note that you can use this at range, so archery builds can ensnare a target, then either wear them down or shift their attention to other foes. It’s a Strength save, which means that most spellcasters and many agile enemies will have trouble with it, but big melee brutes will probably resist it. After the initial save, it takes an Action and and a Strength (Athletics) check (not a save) to escape, and the target takes damage every round, so they’ll likely want to escape quickly. The damage scales linearly with spell level, so this remains a powerful and efficient use of a spell slot throughout your career, but restraining the target is much more impactful than the damage itself. Ensnaring Strike is also an excellent counter to flying enemies because being restrained causes creatures which fly nonmagically to fall, which means that if you shoot a griffon or something it’s going to take a pile of falling damage.

entangle|phb.name: Entangle
entangle|phb.summary: A great area control spell at any level. Strength saving throws tend to be low for any creature that isn’t a gigantic Strength-based brute, so it’s easy to restrain even high-level enemies. However, it requires Concentration so you can’t easily combine it with things like Hunter’s Mark.

fog-cloud|phb.name: Fog Cloud
fog-cloud|phb.summary: An excellent way to cover your escape, but you can’t see through the fog any better than anyone else, so don’t expect to fight in this without some other advantage most of the time. Fog Cloud can be a way to negate Advantage if your enemies have the upper hand, so if you’re facing enemies who are invisible, hidden, or have some other source of Advantage, Fog Cloud can take that away, effectively leveling the playing field so that no one can see each other. Such situations are rare, but it’s nice to know that there’s a countermeasure when those situations do arise.

goodberry|phb.name: Goodberry
goodberry|phb.summary: An excellent resource, both in terms of healing and utility. A Druid can usually spare a prepared spell so that they can dump spells into Goodberry at the end of the day, but that may be harder for a Ranger since you get such a small number of spells known. Still, dumping your spell slots into a pile of goodberries the day before you leave on an adventure will give you a helpful pad of hit points that you can quickly use to heal after combat without resorting to a short rest.

hail-of-thorns|phb.name: Hail of Thorns
hail-of-thorns|phb.summary: This shouldn’t be a go-to option, but it’s a nice way to handle tightly-packed groups of weak foes. Just don’t rely on it too heavily, as it will eat your spell slots quickly without a big payoff.

hunter-s-mark|phb.name: Hunter’s Mark
hunter-s-mark|phb.summary: The Ranger’s bread and butter, and required to benefit from many of the Ranger’s class and subclass features. Many rangers will spend the bulk of their time using Concentration on Hunter’s Mark while they focus upon single foes before switching to the next foe. As a Ranger, your Favored Enemy feature gets you a pool of free castings of Hunter’s Mark, which allows you to save your spell slots for other things without losing chunks of your class. Hunter’s Mark taking so much focus in the design of the DnD 5.5 Ranger is a significant pain point in the class’s design. Unfortunately, there isn’t a way around it without giving up class and subclass features, though not all subclasses require Hunter’s Mark to the same degree. As you gain levels, you may find that other Concentration spells like Elemental Weapon and Summon Beast are more impactful uses for your Concentration.ezstandalone.cmd.push(function () { ezstandalone.showAds(180); });

jump|phb.name: Jump
jump|phb.summary: A great boost to your mobility with a Bonus Action casting time. You can’t afford to use this in every encounter, but it’s great if you need to get past obstacles or hazards.

longstrider|phb.name: Longstrider
longstrider|phb.summary: A helpful buff for highly-mobile characters, and with an hour-long duration it can be a great use of low-level spell slots once your 1st-level spells start lagging in combat.

snare|xgte.name: Snare
snare|xgte.summary: Good for setting a trap, or if you’re resting somewhere dangerous with a convenient choke point like a narrow hallway. Targets are restrained for at least one round, which is hopefully enough for you to fight your way out of your bedroll and grab a weapon.

speak-with-animals|phb.name: Speak with Animals
speak-with-animals|phb.summary: Situational, but sometimes the only witnesses are wild animals and you just need a clue from your local family of squirrels. Fortunately, you can cast it as a Ritual, so it won’t cut into your spell slots.

zephyr-strike|xgte.name: Zephyr Strike
zephyr-strike|xgte.summary: Cast it as a Bonus Action, and you get the benefits of Disengage for the duration of the spell. You can also end the spell early for a boost of speed and a singled buffed attack. If you’re built to fight at range and something gets uncomfortably close to you, turn this on, step back 5 ft., shoot it to express your distaste, then run away.

aid|phb.name: Aid
aid|phb.summary: With an 8-hour duration and three targets, this is a staple buff that’s worth casting literally every day. Keep in mind that this actually increases the targets’ hit point maximum, so temporary hit points can be added, too. Aid’s casting time allows it to be used in combat, which is unusual but offers an interesting option. With three targets and a 30-foot range, you can cast it to both buff and heal your allies during combat. Targets’ current hit points and hit point maximum both increase, so allies at 0 hit points are healed in addition to having their hit point maximum raised, thereby allowing Aid to serve a similar function to Mass Healing Word. However, since spells don’t stack with themselves, it’s hard to repeat this trick. You’ll need to cast Aid again using higher-level spell slots, which can get expensive quickly, so Mass Healing Word is probably better if Aid is already running and if Mass Healing Word is an option for your party.ezstandalone.cmd.push(function () { ezstandalone.showAds(181); });

air-bubble|unknown.name: Air Bubble
air-bubble|unknown.summary: Only situationally useful, but the 24-hour duration means that you can cast it before a Long Rest and still enjoy the effect all day.

animal-messenger|phb.name: Animal Messenger
animal-messenger|phb.summary: Situational and less reliable than similar spells like Sending, but it’s also a spell level lower than Sending and it’s a Ritual. If you know that your recipient is going to be wherever you send your message, this works fine. Unfortunately, the recipient doesn’t get to respond.

barkskin|unknown.name: Barkskin
barkskin|unknown.summary: The best AC that the Druid can get until you can afford half plate or you get to 20 Dexterity. Not essential, and it will become obsolete, but it may be a useful AC buff depending on your stats.

beast-sense|phb.name: Beast Sense
beast-sense|phb.summary: The intent is that you will use this to scout an area using an animal. Maybe you cast Speak With Animals on it, then send it to explore somewhere and use Beast Sense to get a first-hand account. If you’re desperate, you might also use this on an animal and carry it around to help address issues like blindness, deafness, or your own lack of Darkvision. Your DM might reasonably impose Disadvantage on things like attack rolls when doing this due to the uncomfortable shift in perspective, but if you’re truly desperate it might be enough.

cordon-of-arrows|phb.name: Cordon of Arrows
cordon-of-arrows|phb.summary: With a 1-action casting time you might actually be able to use this in combat, but the damage is really low (compare 1d6+Dex twice with Extra Attack to a total of 4d6 from Cordon of Arrows), so the intent is clearly to use this to lay ambushes or to protect an area where you’re resting. Unlike similar options like Alarm and Snare, this doesn’t make a significant amount of noise when it goes into effect, so consider tying a bell to each piece of ammunition after you cast the spell so that you now when it’s triggered. There’s nothing preventing you from casting this multiple times, but the rules for stacking may disallow you from casting it in the same space multiple times. If you have a bunch of spell slots before you take a Long Rest, you could spend them on Cordon of Arrows to create an exceptionally dangerous area for intruders. Unfortunately, there’s no way to exclude your allies from this or to end the spell early, so be careful not to let allies stumble through the area.

darkvision|phb.name: Darkvision
darkvision|phb.summary: Fantastic at any level. 8-hour duration, no Concentration, and almost nothing in the game can match 150 feet of Darkvision. If you can afford the spell slots, cast this on everyone in the party who doesn’t get it from their race.

enhance-ability|phb.name: Enhance Ability
enhance-ability|phb.summary: Fantastic and versatile. Using this to buff Charisma for your party’s Face will make any social situation go a lot better.

find-traps|unknown.name: Find Traps
find-traps|unknown.summary: Too expensive and too imprecise. Invest in Investigation.

gust-of-wind|phb.name: Gust of Wind
gust-of-wind|phb.summary: Potentially a great way to shove enemies around, but at 15 ft. per round enemies will frequently be able to walk back the distance they were pushed without issue. Your best bet is to push enemies into area control effects, but since Gust of Wind requires your Concentration you may have trouble creating effects to use.

healing-spirit|xgte.name: Healing Spirit
healing-spirit|xgte.summary: Likely not good enough to replace healing from a Short Rest when your party is in rough shape, but very efficient for the spell slot if your Wisdom modifier is high. It’s not nearly as fast as Cure Wounds and requires Concentration, so it’s not great in combat, but it’s decent between fights if you don’t have time to rest. The total healing goes up by 1d6 times your spellcasting modifier per spell level past level 2, so you can double the healing by using a level 3 slot. That’s better scaling than Cure Wounds, but remember that you’re trading time for the extra healing per spell slot.

lesser-restoration|phb.name: Lesser Restoration
lesser-restoration|phb.summary: Situational, but a situation that comes up often.

locate-object|phb.name: Locate Object
locate-object|phb.summary: Too situational, and too easy to counter. Anyone with any knowledge of magic that’s trying to hide something will wrap it in lead.

magic-weapon|phb.name: Magic Weapon
magic-weapon|phb.summary: If your game uses magic items, you may never need this. If it doesn’t, this is essential. A bonus to your attacks makes your damage output multiplicatively more reliable. With a 1-hour duration and no Concentration, one casting provides a lot of value from one of your few spell slots.

pass-without-trace|phb.name: Pass without Trace
pass-without-trace|phb.summary: A +10 bonus in a game where most characters max out at +11 is huge. The bonus is enough to offset problems like a fighter in full plate armor. But remember: this is not invisibility. You can’t cast this and crouch down in plain view and magically disappear. I hear that mistake being made constantly on podcasts. A +10 bonus doesn’t negate line of sight rules. You still need cover or something.

protection-from-poison|phb.name: Protection From Poison
protection-from-poison|phb.summary: Situational, but poison is common across the full CR range, so this is a fantastic defensive option at any level. The 1-hour duration means that you can get a lot of mileage out of a single spell slot even if you cast it ahead of time.

silence|phb.name: Silence
silence|phb.summary: Verbal components are extremely common in spells, including many that spellcasters frequently use to escape dangerous situations. If you can trap an enemy spellcaster in place (such as by having an ally grapple them) and drop Silence around them, you’ll significantly limit their options. In the 2024 rules, spellcasting enemies will have combat actions that aren’t actually spells and which will ignore Silence, but you’ll still limit some of their best options.

spike-growth|phb.name: Spike Growth
spike-growth|phb.summary: 2d4 damage every 5 feet, and it’s every time the creature “travels”, not every time the creature moves. So if you push or pull the creature, they take damage. A 20-foot radius spread is a fairly large area, too, so you can easily affect whole rooms or long stretches of hallway.

summon-beast|phb.name: Summon Beast
summon-beast|phb.summary: The lowest-level Summon spell. With a 1-hour duration you can get a ton of mileage out of a spell slot, and the beasts are very effective in combat. If you have other melee allies, throwing one of the beasts with Pack Tactics alongside them can yield a lot of consistent, reliable damage. The Air beast has Flyby, which is appealing if you need a more durable version of the owl familiar’s hit-and-run Help trick, but won’t be as effective offensively as the Land and Water options. Summon Beast has an odd place in the Ranger’s tactics. It competes for your Concentration with Hunter’s Mark, but the beast deals 1d8+6 (avg. 10.5) damage per turn with a level 2 spell slot. Hunter’s Mark, assuming two attacks, deals 2d6 (avg. 7). Summon Beast also puts a body on the field to take damage in place of the actual party mmbers. In most cases, a summon is a better use of a spell slot than HUnter’s Mark, which is especially frustrating because many of the Ranger’s class and subclass features requirey ou to have Hunter’s Mark running. For more help, see our Practical Guide to Summoning Spells.

tortoise-shell|drops.name: Tortoise Shell
tortoise-shell|drops.summary: Only situationally useful. If you need an ally to block a choke point, this could be a helpful defensive boost. Otherwise, characters typically want the mobility to respond to problems, and the +1 AC isn’t worth Concentration. Strongly consider Barkskin before casting this.

ashardalon-s-stride|ftod.name: Ashardalon’s Stride
ashardalon-s-stride|ftod.summary: Bonus Action casting time, and the damage doesn’t allow a save. This is similar in concept to Zephyr Strike, but you get free damage in exchange for a considerably higher spell level. The damage may not be huge by this level, but in encounters with numerous enemies this can add up quickly.

conjure-animals|phb.name: Conjure Animals
conjure-animals|phb.summary: Portable, good damage, and a 10-minute duration. The pack of animals is 10 feet across and the damage effect extends 10 feet from the pack, so the area is a square that’s 30 feet across. You move the area without spending any sort of action, so you can still use the rest of your action economy for other cool stuff. Much like Summon Beast, Conjure Animals has a weird place in the Ranger’s tactics. It doesn’t last as long, but the 3d10 damage will easily exceed Hunter’s Mark, especially when facing multiple enemies.

conjure-barrage|phb.name: Conjure Barrage
conjure-barrage|phb.summary: A massive 60-foot cone, a great damage type, and decent damage. It won’t deal as much total damage as Conjure Animals over the course of a fight, but it’s good burst damage if you catch a bunch of enemies clustered close together.

daylight|phb.name: Daylight
daylight|phb.summary: A Continual Flame, Light, or even a torch is typically sufficient, but sometimes you need to light up larger areas like dark battlefields or massive caverns. This also dispels magical darkness of 3rd level or lower, which is great if you’re fighting enemies like drow which can produce magical darkness. Since it produces sunlight, you can use this offensively against enemies like vampires and enemies Sunlight Sensitivity like drow.

dispel-magic|phb.name: Dispel Magic
dispel-magic|phb.summary: Every party needs someone who can cast Dispel Magic. It’s simply too important to forgo.

elemental-weapon|phb.name: Elemental Weapon
elemental-weapon|phb.summary: Not significantly better than Magic Weapon, a spell level higher, and it takes Concentration. Unfortunately, you can’t use both. Instead, you can cast Magic Weapon and Hunter’s Mark to get the same attack bonus and more additional damage.

flame-arrows|eepc-xgte.name: Flame Arrows
flame-arrows|eepc-xgte.summary: This is a waste of a spell slot. It amounts to at most 12d6 damage, which is a tragic waste of a 3rd-level spell slot. If you somehow manage to hit one target with all 12 arrows, you’ll do more damage than Fireball. But you have to somehow hit with a bunch of arrows or pass them off to someone who will, and following the typical attack vs. AC progression means that a player will hit something like 65% of the time, which means you’re getting 65% of the maximum damage, so something like 7d6. At that point, Erupting Earth is better.

lightning-arrow|phb.name: Lightning Arrow
lightning-arrow|phb.summary: Basically a better version of Hail of Thorns, but the damage is rarely good enough to justify the spell slot so save this for when you have a big group of enemies in a small area. 5 or more seems like a good number.

nondetection|phb.name: Nondetection
nondetection|phb.summary: Good, but not totally essential. Divination spells include things like See Invisibility, so if you or your party relies on invisibility of any kind this protects from several magical countermeasures to both stealth and invisibility. However, most enemies aren’t spellcasters and won’t have access to those divination options, so you can’t justify casting this every day. The spell also has an expensive material component specifically to deter you from casting this all the time. Still, with an 8-hour duration, if you need this spell it’s going to do exactly what you need it to do.

plant-growth|phb.name: Plant Growth
plant-growth|phb.summary: Situational. Outside of normal adventuring activities, the ability to enrich land to double crop yields is very useful. But DnD is a game primarily about adventuring, and the option to make an area of plants overgrown is the more important option for most adventurers. In most cases, Entangle will work fine if you just need to slow your enemies down, but Plant Growth doesn’t expire, so those plants remain difficult to walk through until someone clears the plants (which may requires hours of chopping and/or burning). The spell also doesn’t specify that the plants grow along the ground or surfaces, so RAW it can create a sphere of plants, creating super-difficult terrain extending 100 feet into the air, potentially engulfing flying enemies. The math on Plant Growth’s speed reduction is impressive. Since most creatures have a speed of around 30 feet, moving at 1/4 speed means that they can move one 5-foot square and be left with 10 feet of movement that won’t get them anywhere (unless they dash or something). Jeremy Crawford has clarified that Plant Growth doesn’t create difficult terrain, so it’s possible that difficult terrain would stack with Plant Growth, but I personally think that’s not how it’s intended to work. Plant Growth specifies that “a creature moving through the area must spend 4 feet of movement for every 1 foot” while the difficult terrain rule specifies that “moving 1 foot in difficult terrain costs 2 feet of speed”, and since those two statements conflict I think you’re intended to use whichever effect is greater rather than stacking them or multiplying them or something. While it’s not discussed in the text of the spell, it seems likely that Plant Growth would also impede vision. If you turn a nicely-tended hedge into a 100-foot-radius hemisphere of super-difficult terrain, there’s clearly enough stuff in the way that seeing through it is difficult. This would necessarily mean that creatures inside the area would likely be concealed to some degree, so don’t expect to drop Plant Growth on an enemy and then spend the next several turns spraying them with cantrips until they fall down.ezstandalone.cmd.push(function () { ezstandalone.showAds(182); }); Plant Growth’s problematic limitation is that it requires plants to be in the area. However, there doesn’t seem to be any restriction on how many or how large these plants must be (just that they must be “normal”, whatever that means), and where there’s lack of clarity there’s room for shenanigans. For example: you might carry around a potted plant and throw it into the area to provide the necessary plant life to support the spell. Plants like mint or clover can fit into a small pot, and when you make them grow you get a pretty and pleasant-smelling field of super-difficult terrain. If your DM scoffs at the idea of 100-foot-tall clover patches, consider carrying a bonsai tree or some other plant which would normally be very tall (though a bonsai might not qualify as “normal” since we don’t know what that word means here).

protection-from-energy|phb.name: Protection From Energy
protection-from-energy|phb.summary: An important, staple defensive option, but it’s single-target and requires Concentration, so you can’t afford to keep it running constantly.

revivify|phb.name: Revivify
revivify|phb.summary: Everyone who is capable of casting this should keep it handy. It’s simply too good to forgo.

speak-with-plants|phb.name: Speak with Plants
speak-with-plants|phb.summary: Situational. If you encounter plant creatures, this may allow you to handle them nonviolently.

summon-fey|tcoe.name: Summon Fey
summon-fey|tcoe.summary: The summon options do little to improve upon Summon Beast. For more help, see our Practical Guide to Summoning Spells.

water-breathing|phb.name: Water Breathing
water-breathing|phb.summary: Situational, but crucial when you need it. Fortunately, it’s a Ritual, so it should never eat a spell slot.

water-walk|phb.name: Water Walk
water-walk|phb.summary: Usually flight is a better option than walking across a liquid. This can be cast as a Ritual, but it’s not useful often enough to prepare it if you don’t know for sure

conjure-woodland-beings|phb.name: Conjure Woodland Beings
conjure-woodland-beings|phb.summary: Fantastic for melee builds. Area damage in an Emanation. Conjure Woodland Beings Disengage as a Bonus Action so that you can easily move between targets without provoking Opportunity Attacks, and your Action is still available for attacking once the spell is running. Ranged builds could use similar tactics, but you may prefer to remain at a safer distance. Conjure Beasts may also be a better choice because you can move it from a comfortable distance, though it will deal less damage than Conjure Woodland Beings.

dominate-beast|phb.name: Dominate Beast
dominate-beast|phb.summary: By the time you can cast this, beasts have stopped being a threat.

grasping-vine|phb.name: Grasping Vine
grasping-vine|phb.summary: Put the vine on a ceiling and use it to haul a creature off the ground. If they break the grapple, they fall and take damage, then you can grab them again. If they stay still, you and your party have an easy target that can’t run away. If your party can place an inexpensive ongoing damage effect like Create Bonfire, you can step behind cover and wait. Upcasting the spell allows you to target more creatures, keeping this relevant at any level against any Huge or smaller enemy that struggles to fight at range.

guardian-of-nature|phb.name: Guardian of Nature
guardian-of-nature|phb.summary: This is a challenging spell. The benefits are great, but the duration is short and the spell’s effectiveness depends heavily on how you’re built. Primal Beast is clearly intended to be the scary offensive form, but a druid making Strength-based melee attacks is either a poorly built druid or they’re using Wild Shape. Great Tree is usually the better option: advantage on Dexterity- and Wisdom-based attacks covers important options like daggers, but also covers anything you can use with Shillelagh. The temporary hit points will help compensate for your poor AC, and the area of difficult terrain will help you keep enemies in convenient melee range. Circle of the Moon Druids can get some use out of Primal Beast, but it has a Bonus Action casting time and a 1-minute duration, so until you get Beast Spells at 18th level it’s hard to get both effects going at the same time and you have at most 9 rounds to actually use the effects. Circle of the Moon can choose to Wild Shape as either an Action or a Bonus Action so you can start both effects in the turn, but you won’t be able to do much else in that turn. During the remaining 9 rounds you’ll be very effective, but it’s still only 9 rounds.ezstandalone.cmd.push(function () { ezstandalone.showAds(183); });

locate-creature|phb.name: Locate Creature
locate-creature|phb.summary: More effective than mundane tracking, but the 1,000-foot range can be a problem if the target is actively fleeing from you. If you’re going to use this, be sure that you’re moving faster than your target.

sticks-to-snakes|drops.name: Sticks to Snakes
sticks-to-snakes|drops.summary: This is effectively a summoning spell which summons 4 CR 1/8 creatures. By the time you can cast this, that’s utterly useless. The best-case scenario is using this on wooden items that enemies are carrying. You can’t use it on magic items, so you can’t use it on the enemy wizard’s magic staff, but you can use it on mundane enemy weapons like spears. Most enemies use nonmagical weapons even if their attacks are magic, so this could be occasionally useful through the whole level range. But that depends on your enemies’ weapon selection, which is difficult to predict, so this is only situationally useful.

summon-elemental|phb.name: Summon Elemental
summon-elemental|phb.summary: If you just need a body in a fight, or if you need a creature that can burrow, this is great. Otherwise, you may find Summon Beast or Giant Insect to be more effective. For more help, see our Practical Guide to Summoning Spells.

alustriel-s-mooncloak|frhof.name: Alustriel’s Mooncloak
alustriel-s-mooncloak|frhof.summary: This is a good spell, but you get exactly one level 5 spell slot, and this is too situational to sit on your best spell slot hoping for this to matter.

commune-with-nature|phb.name: Commune with Nature
commune-with-nature|phb.summary: 3 miles isn’t an especially large range, but since this a ritual you can cast this repeatedly as you travel. You might get some useful information, but your DM (and your party) might get sick of sitting around waiting for you to perform the ritual every time you travel 6 miles. You might be able to get away with performing this from the back of a wagon or something, which would let you cast it repeatedly without slowing things down.

conjure-elemental|phb.name: Conjure Elemental
conjure-elemental|phb.summary: Unlike a typical summon spell, this conjures an immobile elemental that restrains your enemies. It might be effective if the elemental can reach everywhere within a room, or if you need to hold a choke point for an extended period, but otherwise you’ll do better with other area control spells.

conjure-volley|phb.name: Conjure Volley
conjure-volley|phb.summary: Decent damage and a good damage type. This is the closest that the Ranger gets to casting Fireball. If you can hit a crowd of targets, it’s worth the spell slot even if they pass the saves. The damage is also 1d8 higher than Conjure Barrage cast at the same level, and can be cast from a much safer distance. Unfortunately, full casters can deal considerably more damage by this level, so it will feel underwheling compared to Wizards slinging Meteor Swarm at the same level.

greater-restoration|phb.name: Greater Restoration
greater-restoration|phb.summary: (Optional): A crucial healing option, but if your party has survived long enough to reach this level you almost certainly have access to this already, and you shouldn’t need to learn it permanently.

steel-wind-strike|xgte.name: Steel Wind Strike
steel-wind-strike|xgte.summary: If you have 20 Wisdom, your Spell Attacks are as good as a full caster, which makes this great burst damage. But remember that Rangers only get one level 5 spell slot, so save this for when you can hit a bunch of targets.

swift-quiver|phb.name: Swift Quiver
swift-quiver|phb.summary: Hugely improves your action economy, but since it requires Concentration, you can’t combine it with Hunter’s Mark or most other damage boosts, and it requires a ranged weapon with ammunition, so thrown weapon builds will find no value here. The ideal is to use this with an archery build, have Magic Weapon running, then turn this on in an important fight. Consider a same ranger with a longbow and without Crossbow Expert. For that ranger, two extra attacks doubles their number of attacks for the turn, taking their damage output from 2d8+2d6+10 with Hunter’s Mark (avg. 26) to 4d8+20 (avg. 38), a nearly 50% increase in damage output. We’re again ignoring the possibility of critical hits, fighting style, magic items, etc. but any of those things tip the math further in favor of Swift Quiver. Even if you’re built for melee, Swift Quiver is a great way to switch to ranged combat and deal a bunch of damage. Now consider a high-level ranger with Crossbow Expert, nonmagical hand crossbows, and 20 Dexterity. 4 attacks will deal a total of 4d6+20 (avg. 36), while three attacks with Hunter’s Mark running will deal 6d6+15 (avg. 36). There is some nuance to the math because the extra attack means another chance to score a critical hit, but the difference isn’t big enough to make Swift Quiver worth being a level 5 spell when you can cast Hunter’s Mark as a 1st-level spell. Magic weapons, feats, or class features which add additional damage will make the math favor Swift Quiver more heavily, but I’m not sure how much you would need to justify the difference in spell level between Hunter’s Mark and Swift Quiver.

tree-stride|phb.name: Tree Stride
tree-stride|phb.summary: In a forest this can be a helpful way to quickly travel short distances, but It’s not nearly as effective for short distances as Misty Step, it’s not good for long distances (you can go about a mile total if all the trees line up perfectly and you run a little bit during your turns), and you’re totally limited by the position and species of trees.

wrath-of-nature|xgte.name: Wrath of Nature
wrath-of-nature|xgte.summary: This would be a great spell if you could guarantee that you were in an area with trees, grass, and loose stones every time you fought something. But you can’t do that, and forests are a relatively small portion of most worlds’ environments.

primal-companion|dancing-item-wildfire-s.name: Primal Companion
primal-companion|dancing-item-wildfire-s.summary: Your defining feature, your companion is equal parts pet and weapon. It has a separate pool of hit points to draw damage away from you and the rest of your party, and its attacks do as much damage as yours do. Your beast’s stats are based on your Wisdom modifier, so strongly consider building around Wisdom. Unlike summoned pets which other classes might use (Dancing Item, Wildfire Spirit, etc.), your pet sticks around all the time. You don’t need to summon it or whatever. However, like any other member of your party, it needs food, healing, rest, etc. The abilities to easily revive your beast with any spell slot and to replace the beast after a Long Rest mean that your beast is functionally disposable. If it dies in combat, or if you need to change beasts to change tactics, doing so is nearly as easy as casting a new summon spell.ezstandalone.cmd.push(function () { ezstandalone.showAds(178); }); Commanding your beast monopolizes your Bonus Action. This directly conflicts with casting Hunter’s Mark, which is a significant problem for the Ranger, but your beast’s damage is good enough to make up the gap. This gets a little messy when you pick up Bestial Fury at level 11 and your beast also benefits from your Hunter’s Mark damage bonus, but by that point your beast’s attacks are more impactful than Hunter’s Mark. Expect to use Hunter’s Mark only in encounters against big single foes, otherwise you’ll waste your Bonus Action to move it around when you should be commanding your beast. : Simple and iconic. With 40 ft. land and climb speed, this thing can get around very quickly. The damage will match or exceed a weapon, and Charge allows your companion to knock foes prone if they can get a running start. : Only viable in aquatic campaigns. 5-foot land speed is not enough for your sharktopus to hobble around on land and be effective in combat. If you can somehow get its speed up to reasonable amount (look for spells like Longstrider with long durations which don’t require Concentration), you may be able to make this work on land. If you can do it, the Beast of the Sea’s attacks grapple when they hit, which is a powerful option not normally available to players. : 60-foot fly speed and Flyby. Less hit points than the other options, but with the ability to remain perpetually out of melee reach that’s less of a problem. The damage is also slightly lower than Beast of the Land, but Beast of the Land deals 6.5+PB on average and the Beast of the Sky’s 5.5+PB isn’t noticeably lower. Having a flying companion discourages you from using your companion as a Defender by interposing itself between you and your enemies, but Beast of the Sky’s AC is just as good as the other options and if your companion’s hit points are looking problematic it can use Flyby to withdraw to safety.

beast-of-the-land|unknown.name: Beast of the Land
beast-of-the-land|unknown.summary: Simple and iconic. With 40 ft. land and climb speed, this thing can get around very quickly. The damage will match or exceed a weapon, and Charge allows your companion to knock foes prone if they can get a running start.

beast-of-the-sea|look-for-spells-like-lo.name: Beast of the Sea
beast-of-the-sea|look-for-spells-like-lo.source:
look for spells like Longstrider
				with long durations which don’t require Concentration
beast-of-the-sea|look-for-spells-like-lo.summary: Only viable in aquatic campaigns. 5-foot land speed is not enough for your sharktopus to hobble around on land and be effective in combat. If you can somehow get its speed up to reasonable amount (look for spells like Longstrider with long durations which don’t require Concentration), you may be able to make this work on land. If you can do it, the Beast of the Sea’s attacks grapple when they hit, which is a powerful option not normally available to players.

beast-of-the-sky|unknown.name: Beast of the Sky
beast-of-the-sky|unknown.summary: 60-foot fly speed and Flyby. Less hit points than the other options, but with the ability to remain perpetually out of melee reach that’s less of a problem. The damage is also slightly lower than Beast of the Land, but Beast of the Land deals 6.5+PB on average and the Beast of the Sky’s 5.5+PB isn’t noticeably lower. Having a flying companion discourages you from using your companion as a Defender by interposing itself between you and your enemies, but Beast of the Sky’s AC is just as good as the other options and if your companion’s hit points are looking problematic it can use Flyby to withdraw to safety.

exceptional-training|unknown.name: Exceptional Training
exceptional-training|unknown.summary: The Bonus Action options are fantastic. Disengage will let your companion move out of melee safely, but you want it in melee tanking hits for your less durable party members. Help will give you or an ally Advantage on a high-value attack. Most of the time you’ll default to Dodge, which will significantly improve your beast’s durability. Making your companion’s attacks deal Force damage lets you bypass nearly all damage resistances. Resistance to non-magic weapon attacks is common and becomes more common as you gain levels.

bestial-fury|unknown.name: Bestial Fury
bestial-fury|unknown.summary: Double your beast’s damage output. The bonus damage from Hunter’s Mark is mostly a consolation prize for giving up your beast’s attacks for a turn in order to cast Hunter’s Mark. Don’t rush to cast it just to get the 1d6 damage.

share-spells|unknown.name: Share Spells
share-spells|unknown.summary: This is a fantastic way to share buff spells. You can use options like Cure Wounds, but don’t expect to cast those frequently.

dreadful-strikes|hunter-s-mark-does-too-.name: Dreadful Strikes
dreadful-strikes|hunter-s-mark-does-too-.source:
Hunter’s Mark does, too, but it’s still really
			nice
dreadful-strikes|hunter-s-mark-does-too-.summary: This roughly matches Hunter’s Mark, but with a lot of advantages. The most obvious benefit is that it’s free, but it doesn’t stop there. There’s no action cost. It stacks with Hunter’s Mark’s damage bonus. The damage is psychic, which is rarely resisted. Dreadful Strikes only applies once per target per turn, but if you can hit multiple targets, they’ll all take the bonus damage. It also applies on Opportunity Attacks (Hunter’s Mark does, too, but it’s still really nice). The one drawback is that it doesn’t work quite as well as Hunter’s Mark does when focusing on a single target, so Hunter’s Mark may still be worth casting. Because this applies once per target per turn, you’re motivated to attack multiple targets if that’s an option. Ranged weapons work best for this, though they may be difficult for the high-Wisdom build expected of the Fey Wanderer. More likely you’ll want to use spells like Zephyr Strike and two-weapon fighting to quickly move between and attack multiple targets.ezstandalone.cmd.push(function () { ezstandalone.showAds(182); });

fey-wanderer-spells|unknown.name: Fey Wanderer Spells
fey-wanderer-spells|unknown.summary: The vast majority of the options are only situationally useful, but you do get Misty Step, which is good on exactly 100% of characters. : A strange choice mechanically, but the theme makes sense. Your save DC won’t match a full spellcaster unless you’re using Druidic Warrior to build around Wisdom, and Charm Person doesn’t give you any visual indication that it worked, so you need to be extremely cautious when using it. You don’t get enough spell slots to cast it repeatedly just to be absolutely sure that it worked. : The best teleportation option in combat. : This will lag far behind summons cast by full spellcasters. Your summoned Fey’s AC and hit points will make it frail, and their relatively small number of attacks will mean that their damage isn’t as impactful as you probably want. Still, if you’re built around Druidic Warrior, this is a much better use of Concentration than Hunter’s Mark. Also see the Fey Reinforcements feature, which lets you shorten Summon Fey’s duration in order to remove the Concentration requirement. : Less of a go-to combat teleportation option than Misty Step, but it has better range and doesn’t require line of sight, so it’s more powerful outside of combat or if you need to completely escape an encounter. You’ll still get more frequent use out of Misty Step thanks to its Bonus Action casting time and lower-level spell slot requirement, but Dimension Door can get you through walls and locked doors. : Situational. Not a great option in combat, but out of combat this provides a passably safe way to scout an area or to trick other creatures if mundane stealth won’t do the trick for some reason.

level-2|unknown.name: Level 2
level-2|unknown.summary: A fantastic way to rest safely, and normally exclusive to artificers and wizards. But rangers get very few spell slots, and spending one to take a Short Rest safely is a high cost for the Ranger. Do your best to avoid needing this.

level-3|unknown.name: Level 3
level-3|unknown.summary: It’s unlikely that you have sufficient Wisdom to make any spell which allows a saving throw reliable, so you’ll want to save this for encounters with numerous weak foes.

level-4|unknown.name: Level 4
level-4|unknown.summary: Amazing on any stealthy character. Ideally you’ll never need this because you can rely on Umbral Sight, but if your enemies pull out a torch you can cast Greater Invisibility and remain unseen.

level-5|unknown.name: Level 5
level-5|unknown.summary: Situational, but very helpful when your party needs to go somewhere where the locals are unfriendly.

otherworldly-glamour|unknown.name: Otherworldly Glamour
otherworldly-glamour|unknown.summary: One Face skill and you add your Wisdom modifier to all Charisma checks on top of any Charisma modifier. This is enough to make you an effective Face without high Charisma, but a little bit is still a great idea. You don’t want 8 Charisma dragging you down.

beguiling-twist|often-spellcasters-but-t.name: Beguiling Twist
beguiling-twist|often-spellcasters-but-t.source:
often spellcasters, but there are
			non-spell options too
beguiling-twist|often-spellcasters-but-t.summary: Hilarious and very effective, but likely difficult to use to its greatest potential. The obvious use case is to take charm/fear effects from your enemies and essentially redirect them back at your enemies. That works great, and can lead to scenarios like dragons being frightened by their own Frightful Presence. To make this as effective as possible, you want allies in your party who can reliably pass saving throws against charm/fear effects. These are nearly always Wisdom or Charisma saves, so high scores in those ability scores and proficiency in the saves both help, but also look for racial traits like Brave and class features like Aura of Protection. The less-obvious use case is using this offensively. If you have allies who can produce charm/fear effects (often spellcasters, but there are non-spell options too), you can capitalize on any creatures who pass saves against your allies’ abilities and force another creature to save against Beguiling Twist.

fey-reinforcements|unknown.name: Fey Reinforcements
fey-reinforcements|unknown.summary: Summon Fey once per day for free without the 300gp material component. The fey’s attack bonus is based on your Spellcasting Modifier and the spell is heavily dependent on spell level, both of which are hard prospects for many rangers. But even if it’s not quite as effective offensively as something summoned by a full spellcaster, it’s still an effective pet for up to an hour per casting. The second benefit allows you to cast a shorter version of the spell without the Concentration requirement, but that’s a really hard prospect with the Ranger’s limited pool of spell slots. Note that the free casting per day doesn’t use a spell slot, so it doesn’t conflict with casting a leveled spell on the same turn. That’s rarely going to be an issue with the Ranger’s limited spellcasting, but it can be a very powerful tactical option.

misty-wanderer|unknown.name: Misty Wanderer
misty-wanderer|unknown.summary: Misty Step for free several times per day, and you can even bring a friend along! This makes it easy to rescue your friends from grapples or restraints, and you become very hard to keep in one place during combat.

ambusher-s-leap|unknown.name: Ambusher’s Leap
ambusher-s-leap|unknown.summary: A modest boost to your mobility on turn one. Great for rushing into melee.

deadful-strike|unknown.name: Deadful Strike
deadful-strike|unknown.summary: Dismal. 2d6 damage that only scales up to 2d8 at level 11. A typical Ranger will have 14 Wisdom, so you’ll get to use this twice per Long Rest. You might think “That’s fine, I’ll just raise my Wisdom!”, but it is absolutely not worth the effort. Stalker’s Flurry at level 11 improves this considerably, but, until then, you’re going to save this for critical hits.

gloom-stalker-spells|unknown.name: Gloom Stalker Spells
gloom-stalker-spells|unknown.summary: 4 of these spells are pretty good and one of those is a Wizard/Artificer exclusive. Now, you too can decide that you need an extra-dimensional pocket to short rest in. This only isn’t rated higher because Disguise Self and Fear care about your spell save DC which won’t be as good as a dedicated caster. : Situational. : A fantastic way to rest safely, and normally exclusive to artificers and wizards. But rangers get very few spell slots, and spending one to take a Short Rest safely is a high cost for the Ranger. Do your best to avoid needing this. : It’s unlikely that you have sufficient Wisdom to make any spell which allows a saving throw reliable, so you’ll want to save this for encounters with numerous weak foes. : Amazing on any stealthy character. Ideally you’ll never need this because you can rely on Umbral Sight, but if your enemies pull out a torch you can cast Greater Invisibility and remain unseen. : Situational, but very helpful when your party needs to go somewhere where the locals are unfriendly.

umbral-sight|candles-etc.name: Umbral Sight
umbral-sight|candles-etc.summary: Getting free Darkvision is fantastic on its own, but invisibility to Darkvision is absolutely crazy. Most creatures that will ambush you using Darkvision won’t have a light source in their possession, so you functionally have Improved Invisibility. Even if an enemy finds a light source, if you extinguish it, you’re right back to invisibly murdering them. Invisibility at this level normally comes at great cost: a relatively high-level spell slot, Concentration, and a prohibition against doing nearly anything aggressive with it. This has none of those costs, it just only applies when something is only able to see you because of its Darkvision. This means that we should be trying to be in darkness in combat as much as is physically possible. Work to make sure that everyone else in your party can function without light as well so that enemies are relying on Darkvision wherever possible. While it is incredible, Umbral Sight does have limitations. The feature specifies that it only works in darkness. That means that it doesn’t work if there’s dim light (candles, etc.). It must be actual darkness. It also doesn’t work on things that can perceive you because of truesight, tremorsense, blindsight, etc. Only Darkvision. With that said, in the right conditions, this is one of the best class features in the game.ezstandalone.cmd.push(function () { ezstandalone.showAds(184); });

iron-mind|unknown.name: Iron Mind
iron-mind|unknown.summary: Additional saving throw proficiencies are always welcome, especially when they’re for a commonly-targeted save.

sudden-strike|unknown.name: Sudden Strike
sudden-strike|unknown.summary: Nice if enemies happen to be adjacent to each other. Capitalizing on this is a good idea even if you’re attacking a creature that’s not currently target by Hunter’s Mark.

mass-fear|unknown.name: Mass Fear
mass-fear|unknown.summary: Good, but you probably don’t have the spell save DC to make this reliable.

shadowy-dodge|unknown.name: Shadowy Dodge
shadowy-dodge|unknown.summary: It only works once per round because it consumes your Reaction, but that’s often plenty. The Gloom Stalker thrives on being unseen, so this is powerful insurance if your enemies manage to attack while you’re not in total darkness and also not running Improved Invisibility.

hunter-s-lore|unknown.name: Hunter’s Lore
hunter-s-lore|unknown.summary: You’re going to be running Hunter’s Mark in nearly every encounter, so you’re going to know the Immunities/Resistances/Vulnerabilities of most of the creatures that you face. Of course, you probably can’t do anything with that information since you’re going to be dealing Piercing damage almost exclusively. None of this specifies “damage”, so RAW it appears that you also know if the target has any condition immunities. Unfortunately, Advantage/Disadvantage on saves against a condition aren’t considered Resistance/Vulnerability in 5e.

colossus-slayer|unknown.name: Colossus Slayer
colossus-slayer|unknown.summary: Enemies will spend very little time in combat at full health, and then they’ll be probaly below full health for the rest of their lives, so this damage is easy and consistent. It’s not a ton of damage, but it’s very reliable and doesn’t require any real effort. Because this works once per turn, it also works on Opportunity Attacks. This is very helpful for melee builds, making you a bit scarier to move past even for enemies that aren’t the target of Hunter’s Mark.

horde-breaker|unknown.name: Horde Breaker
horde-breaker|unknown.summary: This is basically the same as the Cleave Weapon Mastery, except that you can’t have already attacked the secondary target. Since you’re stuck focusing on the target of Hunter’s Mark and can’t easily switch targets, you’re going to have a lot of trouble consistently attacking enemies that are within 5 feet of each other. Opportunities to use Horde Breaker will be vanishingly rare. The timing of Horde Breaker alongside the Cleave mastery is slightly complex, but doesn’t create issues. Horde Breaker applies when you make the attack, while Cleave doesn’t apply until after you hit. This means that you can hit the same secondary target with both Horde Breaker and Cleave after making a single attack against your primary target, but none of that actually matters because Cleave only exists on Strength-based weapons and Strength-based Rangers don’t work.

escape-the-horde|unknown.name: Escape the Horde
escape-the-horde|unknown.summary: If you’re relying on hit-and-run tactics or if you’re built to fight at range, this is a good choice. However, Multiattack Defense may still provide better overall protection. If enemies get into melee with you and hit you with Multiattack, Multiattack Defense will protect you against more attacks than Escape the Horse will when you try to move away on your next turn.

multiattack-defense|unknown.name: Multiattack Defense
multiattack-defense|unknown.summary: Almost every enemy that relies on weapon attacks will have multiattack by now. This will provide consistent defense against those creatures. If you’re fighting in melee, this is a great choice. If you’re fighting at range, this will rarely be useful.

superior-hunter-s-prey|unknown.name: Superior Hunter’s Prey
superior-hunter-s-prey|unknown.summary: 1d6 extra damage per turn. This is not mathematically significant. It’s nice that it works on every turn so that it also applies with Opportunity Attacks, but it’s still not enough damage to make a big difference and it also requires that you have a valid secondary target.

superior-hunter-s-defense|a-dragon-s-bre.name: Superior Hunter’s Defense
superior-hunter-s-defense|a-dragon-s-bre.source:
a
		dragon’s breath, a spell, a weapon
superior-hunter-s-defense|a-dragon-s-bre.summary: A fantastic defensive option. Many enemies can only deal one damage type per turn (a dragon’s breath, a spell, a weapon), and the ones that deal multiple types are typically doing something like hitting you with a mace that does 1d6 bludgeoning and a mountain of fire damage or something. This is going to mitigate a ton of damage.

biting-cold|unknown.name: Biting Cold
biting-cold|unknown.summary: Polar Strikes, Frozen Soul, and several of your subclass spells deal Cold damage, so ignoring resistance will be very impactful.

frost-resistance|unknown.name: Frost Resistance
frost-resistance|unknown.summary: Permanent resistance to a reasonably common damage type.

polar-strikes|unknown.name: Polar Strikes
polar-strikes|unknown.summary: A small but consistent damage boost. Biting Cold gets you past damage resistance, too, so this will be consistently effective. Strongly consider taking Cold Caster. Polar Strikes will trigger the save debuff, allowing you apply -1d4 save penalties every turn at no recurring cost.

winter-walker-ranger-spells|unknown.name: Winter Walker Ranger Spells
winter-walker-ranger-spells|unknown.summary: A lot of offensive damage spells that you get too late for them to be exciting, and also Remove Curse for some reason. : Ice Knife is already a mediocre spell. Getting it several levels later than full casters doesn’t make it any better. : A decent save-or-suck, but it’s only situationally useful since it only works on humanoids. : Only situationally useful, and you get it several levels behind full casters. Hopefully your party’s prepared casters can handle this. : Dismal damage and the area control effect only lasts for round. : Decent damage, but fully 8 levels behind full casters, and it’s on a Constitution save.

level-1-spells|unknown.name: Level 1 Spells
level-1-spells|unknown.summary: Ice Knife is already a mediocre spell. Getting it several levels later than full casters doesn’t make it any better.

level-2-spells|unknown.name: Level 2 Spells
level-2-spells|unknown.summary: A decent save-or-suck, but it’s only situationally useful since it only works on humanoids.

level-3-spells|unknown.name: Level 3 Spells
level-3-spells|unknown.summary: Only situationally useful, and you get it several levels behind full casters. Hopefully your party’s prepared casters can handle this.

level-4-spells|unknown.name: Level 4 Spells
level-4-spells|unknown.summary: Dismal damage and the area control effect only lasts for round.

level-5-spells|unknown.name: Level 5 Spells
level-5-spells|unknown.summary: Decent damage, but fully 8 levels behind full casters, and it’s on a Constitution save.

hunter-s-rime|unknown.name: Hunter’s Rime
hunter-s-rime|unknown.summary: A decent amount of Temporary Hit Points, and it adds some more value to your free castings of Hunter’s Mark. It’s still not fun being so locked into Hunter’s Mark, but mechanically it’s good.

fortifying-soul|unknown.name: Fortifying Soul
fortifying-soul|unknown.summary: A bit of healing once per Long Rest. The buff against Frightened is helpful if you know to prepare for sources of fear. This isn’t good enough to be limited to one use per Long Rest. The range limit on this is line of sight. While this is unlikely to be useful, it’s fun to think about peering through a telescope and healing someone miles away from you.

chilling-retribution|unknown.name: Chilling Retribution
chilling-retribution|unknown.summary: Your attacker functionally doesn’t get a turn if they fail the save. They’re incapacitated and can’t move away, so consider binding them in chains/manacles/rope before they recover. It’s only a few times per day, but this is very powerful even if all that you is stab whatever triggered it.

frozen-haunt|unknown.name: Frozen Haunt
frozen-haunt|unknown.summary: Turn into a spooky ice ghost once per Long Rest when you cast Hunter’s Mark. Since you only get to use this once per Long Rest unless you pay a spell slot to recharge it, strongly consider upcasting Hunter’s Mark to get a duration longer than the 1-hour default. : Immunity to Cold damage and some automatic damage to creatures in an area around you. It’s not much damage, but it’s gauranteed as long as creatures are in the radius at the start of your turn. : The ability to move through objects is insanely powerful.

frozen-soul|unknown.name: Frozen Soul
frozen-soul|unknown.summary: Immunity to Cold damage and some automatic damage to creatures in an area around you. It’s not much damage, but it’s gauranteed as long as creatures are in the radius at the start of your turn.

partially-incorporeal|unknown.name: Partially Incorporeal
partially-incorporeal|unknown.summary: The ability to move through objects is insanely powerful.

poison|unknown.name: Poison
poison|unknown.summary: ed is a massive debuff. However, this targets a Constitution save, and Con saves are consistently high. Resistance and immunity to poison are also common.

trip|unless-someone-is-relying-heavily-o.name: Trip
trip|unless-someone-is-relying-heavily-o.source: unless someone is relying heavily on ranged attack rolls
trip|unless-someone-is-relying-heavily-o.summary: Knocking an enemy prone benefits your whole party (unless someone is relying heavily on ranged attack rolls). This is especially useful against flying enemies because falling prone causes most flying creatures to fall.

withdraw|unknown.name: Withdraw
withdraw|unknown.summary: This is at least somewhat redundant with Cunning Action, but it’s still very useful for melee builds. Use Cunning Action to Dash, run into melee, deliver a Sneak Attack with Withdraw, then you can move your full speed away plus the 15 additional feet from Withdraw. This will put you out of range for most melee enemies, making hit-and-run tactics very safe.

daze|unknown.name: Daze
daze|unknown.summary: You gamble much less damage than Knock Out. The effect is smaller, but still extremely impactful, and it works on targets immune to unconsciousness.

knock-out|unknown.name: Knock Out
knock-out|unknown.summary: A huge gamble. 6d6 is a ton of damage to give up, but knocking your target Unconscious takes them out of the encounter for at least one turn. Unfortunately, this targets Constitution saves, which are consistently high, so it’s not reliable. If you and your party can debuff your target’s saves with options like Bane or Mind Sliver, it may be viable, but otherwise this will be unreliable.

obscure|unknown.name: Obscure
obscure|unknown.summary: Most creatures have mediocre Dexterity, and Blinded is a significant debuff. In many encounters, this will be reliably impactful for your whole career.

alert|phb.name: Alert
alert|phb.summary: Never a bad choice, but less impactful for martial characters than for full casters. The Assassin already gets Advantage on initiative, so they should skip this.

child-of-the-sun|lfl.name: Child of the Sun
child-of-the-sun|lfl.summary: Faerie Faerie Fire may be useful for Arcane Tricksters, but you already have easy access to Advantage from Cunning Action, so you’re using it purely to help your allies. Even if you do want this, go for Magic Initiate (Druid) instead.

crafter|phb.name: Crafter
crafter|phb.summary: Neat, but not especially impactful. Crafting mundane gear stops being impactful early in the game as players quickly accumulate enough to afford nearly anything in the Player’s Handbook. This notably omits the Herbalist Kit as a choice, so you can’t even use this to craft Potions of Healing.

cult-of-the-dragon-initiate|frhof.name: Cult of the Dragon Initiate
cult-of-the-dragon-initiate|frhof.summary: Very good, but you can’t afford the Wisdom to keep this effective.

emerald-enclave-fledgling|frhof.name: Emerald Enclave Fledgling
emerald-enclave-fledgling|frhof.summary: Bad. Take Ritual Caster if you want to talk to animals.

harper-agent|frhof.name: Harper Agent
harper-agent|frhof.summary: The Help Action isn’t useful enough to justify this unless you’re a Hobgoblin.

healer|phb.name: Healer
healer|phb.summary: The Thief Rogue has a unique interaction with the Healer feat because you can use Fast Hands to use Battle Medic as a Bonus Action. This is probably the best use of the feat in the whole game.

lords-alliance-agent|frhof.name: Lords’ Alliance Agent
lords-alliance-agent|frhof.summary: Rogues can’t count on consistent crits, and you already have easy access to Advantage on your tactics.

lucky|phb.name: Lucky
lucky|phb.summary: An easy choice on any character. It won’t directly impact your build, but it’s a great default if you don’t need anything else.

magic-initiate|phb.name: Magic Initiate
magic-initiate|phb.summary: A typical build won’t use offensive spellcasting, but buffs like Guidance or Mage Armor might be worthwhile. An Arcane Trickster build could build around Intelligence by relying on True Strike to attack, which trades some of your stealth and skill capabilities for better spellcasting and a scaling damage boost that works with Sneak Attack both in melee and at range.

musician|phb.name: Musician
musician|phb.summary: A great way to contribute to any party.

purple-dragon-rook|frhof.name: Purple Dragon Rook
purple-dragon-rook|frhof.summary: Proficiency in Insight or Persuasion, and give Heroic Inspiration to your whole party once per day. Excellent on any build if you don’t need a different Origin Feat.

savage-attacker|phb.name: Savage Attacker
savage-attacker|phb.summary: Your weapon damage die isn’t a big enough part of your damage output to make this impactful.

shadowmoor-hexer|lfl.name: Shadowmoor Hexer
shadowmoor-hexer|lfl.summary: Even for Arcane Tricksters, 1d6 damage is not worth your Concentration, but Hex also imposes a debuff on ability checks with one ability of your choice. If you choose Wisdom, your target is much less likely to detect you when you hide.

skilled|phb.name: Skilled
skilled|phb.summary: Rogues already get more skill proficiencies than anyone else, but in a small party you may still need more skill coverage.

spellfire-spark|frhof.name: Spellfire Spark
spellfire-spark|frhof.summary: Rogues lean too heavily on their Bonus Action to make this an easy choice.

tavern-brawler|phb.name: Tavern Brawler
tavern-brawler|phb.summary: You should literally never make an unarmed strike.

tireless-reveler|aboh.name: Tireless Reveler
tireless-reveler|aboh.summary: A great choice on literally any character. While it doesn’t set you up for any specific build, Heroic Inspiration is always useful.

tough|phb.name: Tough
tough|phb.summary: If you need this, you need to be using Cunning Action more to keep yourself safely out of reach.

zhentarim-ruffian|frhof.name: Zhentarim Ruffian
zhentarim-ruffian|frhof.summary: Making Opportunity Attacks can effectively double a Rogue’s damage output, and rerolling your Opportunity Attack damage can boost that a bit further. Giving your entire party Advantage on initiative is also a great way to get a Sneak Attack in and hide before enemies can respond.

aberrant-dragonmark|efota.name: Aberrant Dragonmark
aberrant-dragonmark|efota.summary: The Arcane Trickster may get some value out of this even though the Wizard spell list includes almost everything on the Sorcerer’s spell list. To maximize the value of Aberrant Surge, you want to select a level 1 spell which you’ll cast frequently in combat, so pick a staple option like Absorb Elements or Shield which will remain equally effective for your whole career.

mark-of-detection|efota.name: Mark of Detection
mark-of-detection|efota.summary: Almost all of these spells are already on the Wizard’s spell list, and you still need to prepare them.

mark-of-finding|efota.name: Mark of Finding
mark-of-finding|efota.summary: Hunter’s Mark isn’t as impactful as using your Bonus Action to hide. Even the Arcane Trickster won’t find a lot of value here, though you may find Faerie Fire useful if you can’t get Advantage any other way.

mark-of-handling|efota.name: Mark of Handling
mark-of-handling|efota.summary: Arcane Trickster is the only subclass that will find this remotely valuable, and you already get most of the spells. Animal Friendship of low-Intelligence Monstrosities is neat, but not useful enough to make a difference.

mark-of-healing|efota.name: Mark of Healing
mark-of-healing|efota.summary: Decent healing options for the Arcane Trickster. If your party doesn’t have good healing options, this is a good solution.

mark-of-hospitality|efota.name: Mark of Hospitality
mark-of-hospitality|efota.summary: The spells which you’re likely to use are already on the Wizard’s spell list.

mark-of-making|efota.name: Mark of Making
mark-of-making|efota.summary: Magic Weapon’s +X attack/damage bonus will make your single Sneak Attack per turn more reliable, and Arcane Tricksters might get some additional value out of the spellcasting.

mark-of-passage|efota.name: Mark of Passage
mark-of-passage|efota.summary: Access to some excellent spells including Find Steed, Pass Without Trace, and Phantom Steed.

mark-of-scribing|efota.name: Mark of Scribing
mark-of-scribing|efota.summary: The good spells here are already on the Wizard’s spell list, so the Arcane Trickster gets almost no value.

mark-of-sentinel|efota.name: Mark of Sentinel
mark-of-sentinel|efota.summary: Shield is great, but Rogues are unlikely to use Vigilant Guardian, Compelled Duel, and Warding Bond, so the benefits are minor. Shield of Faith is a good buff, but you’re likely concentrating on something that will buff your Rogue stuff rather than buffing someone’s AC.

mark-of-shadow|efota.name: Mark of Shadow
mark-of-shadow|efota.summary: Nearly every spell on the spell list comes from the Wizard’s spell list, but you get a permanent Stealth bonus, Invisibility once per day without a slot, and you can prepare Pass Without Trace. For a class which relies so much on stealth, that may be worthwhile.

mark-of-storm|efota.name: Mark of Storm
mark-of-storm|efota.summary: Largely mediocre, and almost entirely from the Wizard’s spell list.

mark-of-warding|efota.name: Mark of Warding
mark-of-warding|efota.summary: Most of the spells are already on the Wizard’s spell list, and you’re not likely to use the ones that aren’t.

athlete|phb.name: Athlete
